utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a brief message about P6680, the -- initially --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 65 ter 08611 was the exhibit which was to be replaced and it now should be 65 ter 8611a and that replacement has taken -- has been done so there's no -- should be no concerns about that. Good morning, Mr. Bubic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we resume, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave yesterday that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Mr. Traldi will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Traldi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask first this morning very briefly about the time when you were captured. There was fierce fighting between the VRS and Muslim forces in Kotor Varos at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And as for the operation in which you were captured, you heard suggestions after the war or after your captivity that the Serbs had collaborated in that operation; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that from people with whom I was detained. The information has never been checked so most of it is hard to believe but as you know, anything is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you're not personally certain if it's true or not; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There's no way I can be certain of any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn to one of the other things that you heard while you were in captivity. You explain in paragraph 5 of your statement that: "On the 11th of June, 1992, the Muslims and the Croats were preparing a celebration at Borje to which they invited all prominent Serbs. The Serbs did not respond to the call since they had learned that they were to be killed there." Now, you also heard this from Sprzo during your captivity; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And he was the only one who told me that. When I was set free, and allowed to go, I was very curious to find out how true that was. Unfortunately, I could never obtain the exact information and find out whether it was true or not. If it was true, that's awful. If it wasn't, that's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So you presently don't know whether that's true or not; correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you mentioned yesterday that you'd been interviewed a number of times by the military police during the war. You didn't provide this information to them, did you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. In my view, it would have been stupid of me to provide them with -- with information that wasn't checked, that I wasn't sure of. The information that you hear during the war and that you can be absolutely sure of is few and far between so it shouldn't be shared, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, related --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you said it would be stupid to tell something which was not verified when you were interviewed at the time. Well, in your present statement, where it is still not verified, you have apparently no hesitation to tell us even without telling us that it's just what you heard and not what you know has happened. Would you consider that stupid then as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hesitate to say that it is stupid but yes, it is because sharing information that is not reliable, speculate on things is useless. It doesn't make much sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course therefore, I ask you why you apparently did it to inform us. Did you tell the Defence that it was just what you heard and that you're not certain about what happened, that is, that Serbs did not respond to the invitation and that they even had found a list of those who had to be killed. Did you tell the Defence that it was just what you heard from one person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only the Defence. Whenever I had an occasion to talk about that, I told everybody that that was what I heard. I repeat, yet again, that this information has never been verified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It doesn't appear in your statement that it's just what you heard which is unverified. But let's move on. But for -- whenever you're questioned about any matter, always tell us if it is your personal knowledge or personal observation or whether it's something you heard and, if so, from whom you heard that. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, in this respect, you also discuss in the same paragraph the meeting of the Serb Municipal Assembly on the 11th of June at which you say the decision was taken to take over power in Kotor Varos. Did you attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The Chamber's received evidence, and I refer, for instance, to exhibit P4235, that the takeover was planned at least several days in advance. Do you know whether that's true or not?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to turn to events on the 11th of June. I'm going to ask you about three people first. Anto Mandic, the chair of the National Defence Council in Kotor Varos before the war; Nedeljko Maric, the police commander; and Miro Petrusic, the secretary for national Defence. They were all arrested on the 11th of June, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, what was the third name? I did not hear you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The third was Miro Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew the first two by sight. As for Miro Petrusic, the name doesn't ring a bell, or rather I heard that they were taken for an interview to the Kotor Varos police station. Why they were taken there and by whom, how long were they kept there, I know nothing of those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, at this time you were guarding Kocka 1, 2 and 3 in Kotor Varos; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Those buildings were about 200 metres away from a place called the Pilana sawmill; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, do you know if any of the three men I just mentioned were taken to the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And to complete my questions about them, Mr. Mandic, Mr. Maric and Mr. Petrusic, do you know their ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mandic was a Catholic, the second person was also a Catholic and as for the third one, I don't know. But it would be my assumption that he was too, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Why would that be your assumption?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you judge by the first and last names. If you look at their names, you can more or less guess which ethnic group they belong to. That's why I assumed that they were all Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you say Catholic, that means they were Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But over there in our popular lingo, we call them Catholics. As a matter of fact, they're Croats of Catholic provenance, Christians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to the sawmill briefly, you knew there were people being kept in the sawmill; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honestly, I didn't. But I did hear that people were brought there after having expressed a wish to move out, to go somewhere. It was some sort of a collection centre where they would be safe, where nobody would touch them before they left the territory of Kotor Varos. Again, I heard that. I wasn't there. You couldn't see that location from the building where I was although it was not that far. However, what I'm telling you is only what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to follow up a little bit on the answer you've just given. The people who you heard were brought there after having expressed a wish to move out, those were civilians; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And do you know how long they would stay there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A day or two. Until the transport was organised for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the transport, what you heard was that was to take them out of Kotor Varos; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And it would take them into Muslim territory.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, there were also soldiers from the 22nd Brigade of the VRS active in Kotor Varos around this time, right, while you were standing guard?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sure. At the time you were standing guard in front of buildings, Kocka 1, 2, 3, there were also members of the 22nd Brigade moving around in Kotor Varos; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soldiers did move about, but I can't tell you what brigades they were from. However, it would have been logical if they were only soldiers from the Kotor Varos Brigade. I'm not ruling out a possibility that there were also soldiers from the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Were those soldiers also standing guard in front of buildings?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could you tell what their task was?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they had a specific task. They saw each other in passing, I believe. I don't know whether they went to apartments, houses, whether they moved about from there. But none of us who were there had any other tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, some people were tasked with going into buildings; right? Going into apartments, going into houses.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were things of that kind but again, I think that it was done only when it was found out that people had weapons and they were not supposed to have them, and things like that. But this is just me guessing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You do know that people were tasked with going into buildings, going into apartments, going into houses, and that you could see individual people being taken out of the buildings; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that that was their task. Nobody told me that. However, there were cases when I saw that people were indeed being taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You saw people being taken out by soldiers; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was done by the police, both the civilian and military police forces together. I did not see any soldiers taking people out of the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So turning to a different topic, sir, there was also a Catholic church less than 50 metres away from the buildings you were guarding; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right to the building where I resided, at a distance of some 30 metres or so. It is still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You say it's still there. In fact, it burned down on the 2nd of July, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you say it's still there, what you mean is it was rebuilt after the war; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure of that. And it was restored to its original state. It's functioning, Catholics gather there during their church rituals and services and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to turn now to your evidence about Muslims and Croats who were able to stay in Kotor Varos. First, in fact, many Muslims and Croats left Kotor Varos during the war; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You mention Muslims and Croats who were able to stay from three villages, Zabrdje, Garici and Siprage. Now the people in every one of those villages had surrendered their weapons to the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they surrendered the weapons to the police organs and of these three villages, none were literally ever engaged in any activities, combat activities. I think that in the village of Zabrdje not a single person lost their life during the war with the exception of one man, a Croat, who, according to what I heard, opened fire at an ambulance travelling in the direction of Banja Luka and the worst thing of all was that in the ambulance was a little girl of a Croat, the girl was wounded on that occasion and later died of those wounds. So this was the story that circulated around and it's still being told today, that is, that a Croat from that village killed a child, which is worst of all, who was from his own ethnic community.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, another village in Kotor Varos that the Chamber has received evidence swore loyalty to the Republika Srpska, another non-Serb village, was Hanifici. Now, in fact, in Hanifici the residents weren't as fortunate as the residents of Zabrdje, Garici and Siprage, were they?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably they were not. Probably not. Although I hardly know anything about that village. I had some acquaintances there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did those acquaintances tell you that a group of Muslim civilians there were gathered in the local mosque, were shot, and the mosque was then set on fire. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I heard about that. I heard about that. But I don't know exactly when that happened, who did it, how many victims there were. I know nothing about it. After all, even if there was a single victim, that would be too many and if there were multiple victims then it's really regrettable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 02566. Just for the sake of the transcript, 02566.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now returning to the issue of whether Muslims and Croats stayed in Kotor Varos, this is an assessment of the security situation in the area of Kotor Varos from the Banja Luka state security department. In the first paragraph, we read: "The security situation in the area of Kotor Varos wartime department has significantly improved compared to the situation at the end of May and the beginning of June 1992, which is evident from the balance of power on the ground." "Since 11 June 1992, when the war in the Kotor Varos municipality broke out, the Muslim-Croatian forces have been defeated and the Serbian population, gaining the upper hand, established Republika Srpska. From the last population census in 1991, out of 10.640 Croats, around 1.000 or 5 per cent remained, out of 11.161 Muslims, around 4.500 or 23 per cent remained, while there are 14.000 or 72 per cent Serbs." And I should point out it's dated the 10th of May, 1993. Do you see that text?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It then says: "Croats remained in the villages of Zabrdje, Podbrdje, Sibovi, Bastina, Novo Selo. There is a small number of them in Vrbanjci and Orahova and a few in Kotor Varos. These are predominantly elderly people who do not pose any real threat. Out of a total number of Muslims who remained in the municipality, most of them are in Siprage and the surrounding villages ..." and then it lists several of those where "where they number about 3.500. They are also in Garici and Curkici. A very small number of them are living in Vrbanjci and Kotor Varos itself. The elderly and children are also predominant in this category but there are also a good number of able-bodied men. We assess that around 400 people are up to 35, and another 250 to 300 up to 55 years old." So my --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So, sir, were you aware that most of the Muslims who were left in Kotor Varos were elderly people or children? Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, frankly speaking, I didn't know that because this kind of information never reached me and it was impossible for me to receive it. However, based on logic, it is possible that those who remained within their homes were either old or very young because this middle group of the range of age, who were of military age, in fact, went and joined certain units. However, as I said at the beginning, this is the information that I am not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You single out in your statement three villages where you say Muslims and Croats could stay in Kotor Varos. I'd put to you that what this document shows is, in fact, the great majority of Muslims and Croat had, in fact, left Kotor Varos by early 1993. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that that is true because it seems to me, according to what I learned by talking to the locals, the majority of Croats left Kotor Varos after the combat activities ended in the area of the municipality, that is to say, after the signing of the Dayton Accords. You don't have to take my word for it, but I heard that Franjo Komarica, the bishop of Banja Luka called upon Croats in the aftermath of the Dayton to leave Kotor Varos to their homeland of Croatia, that there was enough room for all of them there. After talking with a couple of people --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We're beyond I think the question I asked. This document here, the Banja Luka state security department is clearly reporting that out of 10.640 Croats, around 1.000 remained as of May 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say either yes or no. This is what the document says. Supposedly it is authentic and then that's it. As I say, this type of document never reached me. I never had an opportunity to see something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 02566.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 02566 receives number P6808, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Mr. Traldi, I take it that at some point in time, you'll explain to me how 1.000 out of 10.000 is 5 per cent, how 4.500 out of 11.000 is 23 per cent. That's still mathematics which is apparently refers to something different from what I can read here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. I think it may be that those percentages relate to the percentage of total people who remain but I'd want to at least use a calculator before expressing that for certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It seems at least --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The total number is not given here and I can already tell you that it could not be the explanation because 14.000 Serbs remaining whereas the total population was at least -- I'm not talking about Hungarians or Yugoslavs, is at least 14.000 plus two times 10.000 which makes 34.000 and I cannot come up with the 72 per cent Serbs unless it is the new population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I had meant the population as of 1993 but we'll look into it further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then so that we at least understand what you have put to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, remaining in that paragraph, I just direct your attention for a moment to the number of Muslims -- it says around 4.500 remain -- and ask you to remember that for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now if we can turn to exhibit P3217.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is a note from the Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior dated June 27th, 1994. At the top we see the prewar ethnic distribution and then looking lower on the page, we see Serbs, 14.000 approximately, Muslims, 1.800. So looking at those two reports, we've seen another 2.700 Muslims left Kotor Varos between May 1993 and June 1994. There was no combat in Kotor Varos at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which period? Which period did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Between May 1993 and June 1994.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think there was any combat operation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the people who left generally left on convoys headed for Travnik; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part. Although some of them even walked up there towards Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned you, yourself, saw one such convoy passing through the village of Zabrdje in September 1992. And you say in paragraph 19 of your statement that you recognised some neighbours of yours on the convoy. Those neighbours were Muslims and Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, some of the people on the convoy eventually were able to continue to Travnik, some were taken off and taken to Manjaca camp; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard some allegations and speculations on that subject, but my strict task assigned to me by my command was to go there in order to recognise the people that I had seen in the course of my captivity, that is to say, the people who tortured me and ill treated me while they were holding me prisoner. Honestly speaking, I saw only one of them, but since he treated me fairly, I did not want to report him because that would not be a humane act. I didn't want to say anything against that man. However, I came across a lot of civilians, among other things, behind the building where I was residing or where I still live, there's a female neighbour of mine who had one under-aged son and one son who was of age. She met me and she asked me by saying, Obrad, can you find bread somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... material, I think that's in your statement and beyond the scope of the question I asked you. So I'm not challenging your evidence about having given these people bread. I'd simply ask you to focus on the question that I'm asking. Is that all right? Now, you say that -- you describe a task assigned to you by your command. This was an order from the corps command relayed to you via your brigade command; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your task was to look not just for people who'd ill treated you but also individuals who used to have weapons and were on the other side; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No. No. My sole task was should I identify someone who maltreated me, to report this person to the police officer who were present on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 31374, page 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And while it comes up, sir, the police officer you were supposed to report people to, that was military police, right, as you testified yesterday?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were both military and civilian police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What brigade were the military police from?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the light Kotor Varos brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, if we could scroll down to -- starting at line 20. You testified in the Stanisic Zupljanin case about this group and you said, beginning at the end of line 20: "My task was to have a look at these individuals and identify among them those who tortured me, if any of them were, and to see if among them were individuals who used to have weapons and were on the other side." Now, was your testimony in the Stanisic Zupljanin case truthful in this respect?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, time goes by and it has its effects. Now frankly speaking, I don't even remember any longer whether that referred only to those who had ill treated me or perhaps that included some other persons as well. I don't think that's too relevant. The important point is that I didn't see any such persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, what is relevant and is not relevant will be determined by the parties and by the Bench. You don't have express yourself on relevance. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, people, regardless of who had selected them, people were taken off this convoy in Zabrdje as part of this search; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody was taken off at Zabrdje. They only boarded the buses and continued their journey onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So they weren't on the buses, were there people that weren't -- let me rephrase that. I'd put to you there were people that weren't allowed to get back on the buses. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I am not aware of such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Were you aware of what would have happened if you'd identified one of the persons that you were tasked with identifying, what would the military police have done? Or the regular police.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose they would take them for questioning, maybe they would be prosecuted before a court of law or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now finally, could we have 65 ter 31394. And out of caution I'd ask that it not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is an indictment filed in November 1993 and it refers to a group of soldiers in -- all of them are identified by military post VP 2233 Kotor Varos. That was the military post for the Kotor Varos Light Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's right but since it's changed quite a few times, I think that by looking at these names, they were members of the Light Kotor Varos Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now looking below the names, we see the words for the following acts and it reads: "On 28 June 1992, at 1600 hours, upon prior agreement, they came together into the house of" - and then it names a person - "the village of Orahova, drove her to the village of Dubrovci into the house of Obrad Bubic from Maslovari and threatened her with firearms. They raped the victim." And then it gives more details. Now your house in Dubrovci is the weekend cottage you mentioned yesterday; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now and it says they'd gone to Orahova, that was a majority Croat village; right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of this crime that had been committed in your home in Dubrovci?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I learned about it three years ago. The principal accused, Cicmanovic either died or got killed during the war. Anyway, he is no longer living. Bozic is still alive. Markovic one and Markovic two are also still alive. Immediately after I had learned of this crime, I met Ostoja Markovic listed here under number four. As luck would have it, he managed to escape because I had an intention of choking him. And they were or they are currently again the subject of court proceedings for this same war crime and I believe that the main hearing is scheduled for the 7th of October and I received summons to attend as a witness at this trial. You can rest assured, because Ostoja admitted to having committed this crime, he and the others. I don't think it's enough to say that he is a completely sick person, but whatever may be the case, I personally would ask the court to impose the most severe sentence and punishment upon him because my house was built up there for completely different things. It was not made as a place where such heinous crimes would be committed. I condemn that even if they had been committed by my own child. Believe it or not, after all of this, we stopped going there altogether. In addition to that, we had floods in the area, so this house is completely rendered unusable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, just two brief questions to follow up. First, you say proceedings are going on now. So it's true that none of these people were punished during the war for this crime; right? If you know.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, or rather I heard that during the war, they were on trial. There were proceedings instituted against them. How, where, when and how it ended, I don't know. I did hear that there were proceedings against them. I'm glad to hear that they are on trial and that they will be brought to justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And sir, I'd put to you that it was crimes like this and other crimes that made Muslims and Croats feel they had to leave Kotor Varos. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't speak for them and what they believed or didn't believe. In any case, any normal person will stand on its end when they start thinking about war. Many fled without thinking twice in order to save themselves and their families. And of course, if one hears of things like that, the situation gets compounded because whoever heard of a crime of that kind doesn't really think of who the victims were. The most important thing was that the crime happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender this document and that complete my cross-examination. I'd ask that it be placed provisionally under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31394 receives number P6809, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted under seal for the time being. We'll take a break. Mr. Lukic, could you tell us how much time you'd need after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I need probably five minutes, six minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you could consider to cross-examine the witness now if you say it's just five minutes and then we would --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can finish then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then if it's five minutes, then there may be a sixth or seventh minute for a question by Judge Moloto. Let's try to see whether we can conclude the examination of the witness before the break. Well, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Judge Moloto wants to ask first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Bubic, you say these people that were mentioned here on this document are on trial right now as we speak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This must be correct because I received an invitation to appear before the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the proceedings that were initiated by this indictment which was in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know this current proceedings that are taking place, when they were initiated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Some 10 or 15 days ago, I received an invitation to appear at a hearing on the 7th of October or perhaps the 8th of October. Please don't hold me to the date. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And earlier than that, when the proceedings of 1993 had been initiated, you had never been invited to come and testify at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I knew nothing about that. If I'd known anything about that, I would have done something, rest assured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bubic, once again.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Earlier today, you were asked about paragraph 5 of your statement which deals with that plan and the plan was, according to you -- please bear with me. "On the 11th of June, 1992, the Muslims and the Croats were preparing a celebration at Borje to which they invited all prominent Serbs. The Serbs did not respond to the call since they had learned that they were to be killed there." And according to you, Sprzo told you that, that's what you said. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When Sprzo was telling you that, were there any other people around you, anybody, for example, from his unit?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In that case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's pretty leading, not only asking whether others were present but already identify who possibly would have been there. That's an examination in chief is not what we expect you to do. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On transcript page 17, lines 8 through 10, my learned friend Traldi asked you I will read the question in English and it will be interpreted [In English]: "I put to you that there were people that weren't allowed to get back on the buses. That's true, isn't it? Your answer was: "I don't know. I'm not aware of such instances." [Interpretation] Did you personally see that anybody was banned from getting on the bus?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And as for the last document which is no longer on the screen, we were looking at it. It was an indictment which was issued in 1993 by the Military Court in Banja Luka. Did anybody ever tell you about the requirement from you as a member of the TO or the military to plunder, rape, loot, did you ever receive an order of that kind?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: God forbid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was rape part of the policy of either the political or military leaderships of Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD BUBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Not only do I not think so, but I think that it would be insane to find that as part of a specific strategy of either a military or a municipality or anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up a document which is 65 ter 31394. [In English] Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then can we go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Bubic, this concludes your testimony in this Court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered the many questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it, and I'm asking the -- those who understand the language, that what the witness said at the end was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That he has some health issues and that's why he is walking like this and he wishes everybody a good day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's understood. I just wanted to verify that it was irrelevant for the proceedings and it seems to be irrelevant for the proceedings. We'll take a break and perhaps we take a break a little bit longer than usual since we went on for quite a while. We'll take a break and we'll then resume at 20 minutes past 11.00, so a break of a little bit over half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. I did have one administrative preliminary which I think you're already aware of but I'd like to put it on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that -- is it a matter which requires confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: The Prosecution has requested and received revised English translations for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would not mind I have a list of all that and whenever we have a spare moment, we'll deal with that if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have about three documents, I think that needs to be addressed. We do that at a lost moment because it's not that urgent at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you testify, the rules require that you make a solemn declaration. May I invite you to make the solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Davidovic, you will first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You find him to your left, and Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D1623 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, in front of you on the screen, you should be able to see on the left-hand side of the screen --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- a document. First of all, I'm going to ask you whether you provided a statement --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to wait until the question is put to him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you always make a short break between question and answer. You're speaking the same language and the interpreters first have to interpret it for us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see a signature on the document that is before you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see a signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's look at the last page of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see a signature and do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see a signature and I recognise it as mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to revise your statement before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did have an opportunity to read my statement before I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is recorded in the statement, is it truthful?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Everything that is recorded in the statement is what I said and truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would you answer them in the same way?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in principle, I would answer the same questions in the same way or rather in similar way because I would not be able to repeat my answers word for word, but in essence, my answers would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now we would like to tender Mr. Davidovic's statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a point, Mr. Lukic. The date of birth in paragraph 1 of the statement is different from the cover sheet by ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In B/C/S it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the English it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The difference is between the B/C/S and English version so you cannot say it is not in the B/C/S. It's ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The gentleman signed the B/C/S version so obviously there is a mistake in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So what is the correct one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The correct one is 1947.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness can tell us which is the correct one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let him tell us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In which year were you born, Witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you hear the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you hear the question, Witness? I haven't received an answer yet.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is waiting for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I heard the question and I can answer that I was born on the 18th of March, 1947.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you to Judge Moloto for helping us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1623 receives number D675, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Lukic, before we continue, I would have one item which I'd like to briefly deal with in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Finally. I will not have any questions for this witness. I'll just read his short summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Statement summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll listen to that summary. You've explained to the witness what it is for.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Branko Davidovic testifies about the political situation, ethnic structure, political parties and their programmes in Sanski Most in early 1992. He also speaks about the details regarding the organisation of the referendum for secession and about the plebiscite to stay in the then Yugoslavia. Branko Davidovic states that mobilisation was carried out and the 6th Krajina Light Infantry Brigade was formed in accordance with the law on the national defence. In June 1992 [sic], the 6th Krajina Light Infantry Brigade was deployed in Jasenovac area with a task to protect the local population. On 2nd April, 1992, the 6th Krajina Light Infantry Brigade was transferred from Jasenovac to Sanski Most area. Mobilisation was carried out in Sanski Most. Davidovic was mobilised and deployed in the 6th Krajina Light Infantry Brigade as assistant commander for morale. Davidovic will testify that the media fabricated the role of the Serbs in the events in Sanski Most in the named period. The media reported that the Serbs had seized the power, but the truth was quite the opposite: the truth was that in the elections, the Serbs had won the majority of the seats in the municipal assembly. On the 25th of May, 1992, the unit launched a legitimate search and control of the municipality Sanski Most with the aim to identify and disarm paramilitary units. Some individuals publicly misrepresented this operation, like other similar operations: they depicted it as the Serbian attack against the villagers. But, the intensity of combat and the VRS losses show that Hrustovo village in Sanski Most municipality was a stronghold of the Muslim units. Davidovic underlines this historical context of the events in Sanski Most and speaks about the great number of Serbs killed in World War Second. He also talks about the repeated creation of the similar ethnic formations, which caused the Serbs to fear for their existence. He explains the character of the war in the B and H 1992 until 1995 by depicting the post war ethnic structure of Sanski Most. And that was the short summary of the statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, are you ready to start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before Mr. Jeremy, I just wanted to check with Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic, if you look at page 41, lines 12 to 17, you say in June 1992, the 6th Krajina Light Infantry Brigade was deployed in Jasenovac area with the task to protect the local population. The next paragraph says the 2nd April 1992, the 6th Krajina Light Infantry Brigade was transferred to Jasenovac. It looks like you said something differently here but I'm not sure whether you are corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour it should say in June 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In June 1991. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The 6th Krajina Light Infantry Brigade was deployed in Jasenovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And then in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was transferred from Jasenovac to Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, this being clarified so the public is now aware as well. Mr. Jeremy, if you're ready, you may cross-examine the witness. Mr. Davidovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Jeremy. You'll find him to your right and he's counsel for the Prosecution. And could I already ask you to refrain from too much opinion in your answers, that your statement is full of a lot of opinion. Mr. Jeremy will ask questions of fact and you're invited to stick to facts rather than to opinions, judgements, et cetera. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Davidovic. Now, I'd like to begin by making a few clarifications in my -- for myself in your statement. If we can begin with paragraph 1 you provide some details about your background. Now, in the statement that you provided in the Karadzic case in which you testified earlier this year, you provided some additional details and I'm just going to read those additional details to you now and ask you to confirm whether they are correct. So you stated: "Until 1990, I occupied the following positions, commander of the police station, president of the municipality, chief of public security service, and a director of kindergarten." Now, that is what you said in your Karadzic statement. Is that correct? Do you stand by that today?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all of it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 15 of your -- of the statement in this case, you say that you responded to the call up on the 10th of April, 1992 now at that time you became a battalion commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And I have this call-up papers here with me should you like to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in paragraph 14 you say two months after your call-up, you were appointed assistant commander for morale, legal affairs and information. So that appointment was made on approximately the 10th of June; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, as assistant commander for morale, you reported to the 1st Krajina Corps on for morale issues as they related to the 6th Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And on the basis of the reports that you provided, the 6th corps, Krajina Corps Command would report to the VRS Main Staff on the state of morale in the Sanski Most municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's how it's supposed to be. I don't know whether it was. I sent my reports to the command in charge on the state of morale in the 6th Light Brigade. I assume that they compiled the reports from other units and sent them all to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: We'll now look at a document you discuss in paragraph 16 of your statement and at various other points as well. This is the combat report of the 6th Krajina Light Infantry Brigade for 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P3851 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, this document is undated and it's unsigned. Nevertheless, this is the 1992 combat report that you refer to in your statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's a combat report for the year 1992, the one which I made reference to in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And this document clearly explains the activities of your brigade over the course of 1992; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 13 of your statement, we read: "On returning to Sanski Most, the brigade command installed itself in the village of Lusci Palanka. The brigade command thought that in this way it would help to calm tensions between the divided citizens."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, in connection to that I'd like to look in page 3 of this combat report, page 3 in the English, please, page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I'd like to focus your attention on the subheading "The brigade from 3 April 1992 to 1 September 1992." Now, below this we read, "When the brigade arrived in the territory of Sanski Most municipality, the Serbian people greeted it with enthusiasm and a feeling of security. They were attached to their army and viewed it as their true protector. Contrary to the Serbs, the Muslims viewed the arrival of the brigade with suspicion, resented its presence, and closed ranks around the SDA, forging plans of retaliation against the Serbian population." Now, Mr. Davidovic, this combat report and the section that I just read out sets out the true picture, yes, the brigade did not calm tensions but rather the Serb population viewed it as their true protector and the Muslims viewed it with suspicion, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: In order for this to be correctly understood, the essence is that the Serbs were frightened as a result of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Yugoslavia and especially in Croatia, that the crimes that took place in 1941 and 1942 would be repeated in Sanski Most, that is during World War II and I describe that in my statement. Therefore, that is why the Serbs were delighted and according to what we saw, this is not how the Muslims perceived it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in paragraph 20, you also talk about the worsening of interethnic relations between Serbs on the one hand, and the Muslims and Croats on the other. And you make a reference to a historical event at Sisinja [phoen], in fact you say: "The post-war generations would see for years the blood that had poured out of the graves in which the perished Serbs had been buried which added to the fear that the Serbs might suffer the same fate again." Now, in connection with this, I'd like to look at another portion of this combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 4 in the English and 5 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, I'm going to read a quote from this document and it relates to documents allegedly found by the Sanski Most CSB which we referred to in the preceding paragraph. We read: "The documents found show that they intended to commit genocide against the Serbian people, kill them and expel them, and create a Muslim state in these parts; all renowned Serbs and their families were to be killed and hanged in the park in Sanski Most; Serbian girls and women were to be put in brothels to bear offspring to the Mujahedin and Janissaries; Sharia laws and government were to be introduced as in Iran, male Serbian children were to be circumcised and brought up according to Islamic laws and principles." Mr. Davidovic, this is the information which you provided to your troops as commander for morale; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And rather than calm interethnic tensions and fears for the past, this sort of language, the language that you use in your statements and the language that we saw in this combat report that you helped draft that actually manipulated those fears and increased those ethnic tensions; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't speak to our troops in the same style as written here. This was copied by the public security and national security services from the documents and these were submitted to our security organs. So we copied this verbatim and sent it upward to our command. However, in talking to our troops, we never used this kind of language. On the contrary, we did our best to convince them to forget what had happened in the past and that in the present, it will not be repeated. Therefore, whenever I was able and as well as other officers and especially me as assistant commander for morale to speak to my soldiers, I always spoke to them as a human being, and I always requested that they behave in every possible situation as human beings and not as evildoers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, on the basis of your answer to my question, it seems that you would agree that this language would stoke ethnic tensions between Bosnians and Serbs in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But it's your evidence that this language was not used with your troops; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Never. Never was this language used. Quite the opposite. Let us forget what had happened. Let us preserve as much as can be preserved in terms of peace in the area, and let us leave it up to the politicians and the state to regulate other things, because the Serbs wanted to remain the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, whereas the Croats and Muslims did not want that to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And it's also then your evidence that this combat report for the 6th Krajina Brigade was not made available to the members of that brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, it was not made available to brigade members. It was drafted for the eyes of the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In paragraph 21 of your statement, you state: "I know from some polemics in the media that attempts are being made to present false claims that the Serbs seized power in Sanski Most municipality which is not true." Now, on page 5 of this report, we read the following: "In order to protect socially owned property on the 20th of April, 1992, the brigade took control of all the more important facilities and localities in town." Mr. Davidovic, as your combat report states, the 6th Brigade played a key part in a pre-existing plan to take over power in Sanski Most, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Things came to a head. Everybody was dissatisfied. And one could sense that palpably, it was very clear. The brigade command pursuant to an order of the superior command decided to take the most important features and facilities in the town and in the municipality in order to protect themselves from possible sabotage activities. Whether that was conducive to the takeover of power or not, I don't know. If you would allow me, perhaps I can explain in detail. I would like to start by saying that I don't understand the term "takeover of power by the Serbs," in view of the fact that that administration or that power was established already in December 1990 and it was functioning throughout 1991 and continued to function until the month of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you but we read that in your statement and I will explore with you what I mean by the "takeover of power by the Serbs." Now, in your last answer, you say that -- I'm just going to find it -- that pursuant to an order of the superior command, it was decided to take the most important features and facilities in the town and in the municipality. Now, in paragraph 34 of your statement you say that you're puzzled by the suggestion that your brigade took part in an attack on the Sanski Most municipality. Now, when you speak of your brigade taking important features and facilities in the town, this was on the 19th of April, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: But you would not characterise this as an attack but you agree that important facilities were taken over by your brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't consider that an attack. There was nobody to attack. An order arrived to prevent sabotage activities which were quite possible under such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What the witness states he was puzzled about might not be that much interesting for others. What is important, what this Chamber is puzzled about upon the presentation of the cases by the parties. Again, let's avoid that a witness who says that the takeover of power, that it didn't happen, and then to say that he doesn't know what is meant by a takeover of power, if we are discussing attacks and say well, it was not an attack, we end up in a linguistic battle rather than in an exploration of the facts and that's what the Chamber needs most. And the Chamber is fully able and it also explains my warning to the witness in the beginning of his testimony that is the Chamber is fully able to make a distinction between opinion, judgement, et cetera and a presentation of clear facts. Could you please keep that in mind when you continue your cross-examination, and you are invited to do that after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, we'll take a break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes from now. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, Mr. Jeremy will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, shortly before the break, we were looking at the combat report from the 6th Brigade and we looked at some language in there that referred to, among other things, genocide against the Serbs and you agreed with me that that sort of language would stoke ethnic tensions between Bosnian Muslims and Serbs in Sanski Most; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if things were done that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, you said that in respect to the -- to the combat report that we looked at, that language, that that wasn't distributed to members of your brigade. In connection with that answer, I'd like to show you a document. Now, before I do, your superior officer in the 1st Krajina Corps was Milutin Vukelic, correct, once you became commander for morale and religious affairs in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a colonel. He was a corps member, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P2874.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, we see that this is a report of the 1st Krajina Corps command. It's dated the 21st of May, 1992. And if we go to the last page we see that it is signed by the assistant commander for moral guidance, Colonel Milutin Vukelic. Now, in paragraph 2 of this document, we read, "In such conditions, the Serbian people in BH and Croatia found themselves in the most difficult situation. Even though the oldest and a constituent people, they are exposed to unscrupulous deprivation of their rights: transformation into a national minority and genocide."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we please note the reference in the B/C/S text, where you're reading from, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, and I read the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: On the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please go to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whoa --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to the second page in each document, in fact, in the final page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, just above the signature, we read: "Inform all members of the Army of the Serbian Republic of BH about the contents of this report in the most suitable way." Mr. Davidovic, on the face of this document, it appears to contain the language which you agreed would stoke ethnic tensions between the Bosnian Muslims and the Serbs and we see that -- we see this instruction to inform all members of the army of the Serbian republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So would you agree with me that this report by Colonel Vukelic would, in fact, stir those tensions?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it could have happened as a matter of fact, but when additional explanations were provided to the combatants, that means that one should not necessarily expect any escalations. We were duty-bound to proceed and treat every document from the superior command the same, which means that we were duty-bound to inform our men of the contents of this document. I don't know how we did it, but in general terms I can guarantee you that every document was additionally explained to our men. We told them exactly what was contained in the document and what the contents of the document meant for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on. Now, immediately before the break, you spoke about your brigade securing key facilities in Sanski Most on the 19th of April, 1992. Now, it is correct, is it not, that this securing process had been planned well in advance of the 19th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No command would be serious if it didn't plan its activities in advance and those activities which are indeed or were indeed planned in advance were carried out. There was a group of people which was assigned to secure certain facilities, not entire units. It was done according to our estimates. We estimated how many men were needed to protect a facility from any sabotage actions and destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And this securing was carried out in coordination with the Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. I don't know whether that was coordinated with the Crisis Staff or not. In any case we received an order from our commander to do that. Whether the commander was in communication with the Crisis Staff or not, I am not in a position to tell you because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And in securing these facility, you acted in coordination with the TO and the SJB; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Of course for a territory to be cares free [as interpreted] there should be a certain level of coordination. That coordination did exist to a certain extent. However, we carried our own tasks and I mean us lower-ranking officers and brigade members only pursuant to an order of our chief and commander, I suppose that they issued order to us based on the orders that they, themselves, received from their superior commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to take a look at a document in connection with these events. Before I do, Nedeljko Rasula, he was the president of the Sanski Most municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. His party won the most votes in the multi-party elections and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, please answer the question and leave it to that. A "yes" is an answer to the question. Whether he was married, was elected, it's not asked. Just limit yourself to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P3294. And could we take a look, please, at page 19 in the English, and page 16 in the B/C/S. I'm looking at the bottom half of the English page and the top right side of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, as I mention, this is the diary of Nedeljko Rasula. Before us we see the heading: "Course of action in taking over power and establishing the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most." We see that it is dated the 14th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, towards the bottom of the page in the English --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In fact I think we'll need to go to the next page in the B/C/S, it appears. We see "Security measures to forestall any resistance by the opposite side are given below ..." If we go to the next page in the English, please. And the bottom half of the B/C/S that you're looking at and the top half of the English we see, "Providing security from outside we see there's a reference to the 6th Krajina Brigade, the reserve police units, and we see civilian territorial units.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So the units that you've already mentioned, Mr. Davidovic, but you would agree that this diary entry does suggest coordination with the Crisis Staff in respect to the takeover on the 19th of April, 1992, in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the municipality could plan whatever he wanted and whenever he wanted and although the president of the municipality tried sometimes to give us certain orders and instructions, we never accepted any of those. At that time, during the takeover of power, as you call it, in Sanski Most, the 6th Krajina Brigade did not take part. Our units were deployed at certain facilities and they were in reserve which means that most of the men were actually at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, this entry that we are looking at is entitled "course of action in taking over power and establishing Serbian municipality of Sanski Most," hence my use of the word "takeover".

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Let's look at another entry in this document. Could we please go to page 22 of the English and 14 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, we've already discussed your evidence in respect to, you say, the brigade's aim was to prevent interethnic conflicts and I'd like to look at an entry relating to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Are we at page 14 in the B/C/S? Can we go to the right. One moment, Your Honour, I need to find the right page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We see that it's half a page. If you would move to the left, you may see something else. You see something else but apparently not what you are seeking, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we go forward by -- can we go forward a page, please. And another page, please. And by four more pages, please. I think it's page 19 in the B/C/S. And by one more page, and with a thank you for your patience to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Davidovic, we see that this is a meeting dated the 20th of April, 1992, so that's a day after the takeover of the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have the right one in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is at the very bottom, it says, "Meeting 20th of April". And we now look at the next page where apparently it is reported about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: So we see those present at the meeting is General Talic, Colonel Basara, Major Sarkic [phoen] and representatives of the SDS, SDA and the HDZ. Could we go to page 26 in the English, please, and if we can go to the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I see it's the right side I'd like to focus on. We'll need to go one page back in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, we see here concluding remarks from General Talic at the bottom of the page. And we read: "The JNA Yugoslav People's Army will guarantee the peace of the citizenry and security of property. We are asking for your help."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page in the English, please. We read: "Don't call anyone for help, otherwise you will have Kupres, Bosanski Brod, Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, it's correct, is it not, that General Talic here is issuing a threat at this meeting between representatives of the various parties?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not attend that meeting. I don't know when that meeting took place, who the attendees were. I don't know what was discussed. So I would not be able to tell you what the general had in mind when he said what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. Now, in paragraph 40 of your statement, you say that Colonel Basara was not a member of the Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, he was not a member of the Crisis Staff. Colonel Basara wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I mean Colonel Basara.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to page 40 in the English, please, and it should be 30 in the B/C/S. Yes. Sorry, can we focus on the right side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Sir we see this is a meeting of the Crisis Staff, it's dated the 11th of May, 1992. Item number 1, we see: "Basara awaiting orders from above to become a member of the War Staff, as the Crisis Staff is to be referred to until further notice." Now, Mr. Davidovic, General Talic was Colonel Basara's corps commander; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Now, on this issue of Basara's membership of the Crisis Staff, I'd like to look at another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see P404.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I can tell you Mr. Davidovic, coming up on our screens will be conclusions of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most dated the 30th of May, 1992. Now, we see the conclusions and we see A, towards the top of the page, "The Crisis Staff consists of the following 12 persons, each one having a clear domain of activities." And if you look at number 10, we see Colonel Basara, 6th Krajina Brigade commander. Now, Mr. Davidovic, it's clear from this document that Colonel Basara did get those orders from above and in fact he was a member of the Crisis Staff; yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DAVIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, and Colonel Basara told me several times himself, that he wasn't a member of the Crisis Staff but that he did, from time to time, attend the Crisis Staff meetings, as did I. I don't know if he was actually a member of the Crisis Staff but I do know that he claimed that he wasn't and I am convinced that he wasn't a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The OTP is aware and they have those documents as their evidence where it is clear that Mr. Basara was not a member of Crisis Staff. The documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is not a matter to be discussed in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is misrepresentation of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think as a matter of fact what is presented to the witness is this evidence.
